chapter: Instruments, own band and the Eureka
title: Union, railroad insurance and Illinois Central retirement
summary: He left the union, discusses railroad group insurance, and his 37 years on the Illinois Central ending with a 1956 retirement letter; he took days off to play.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: No, I got out of the union. But now I wouldn't get back. I wouldn't go back, but you can't get the death part, so I wouldn't get the death part. No, see, I didn't pass the age.
Oh, yeah. That's true.
At age, it always got something to do with you.
Mm-hmm. It's hard to get insurance. Yeah. Yeah.

I was in the railroad insurance, group insurance. Mm-hmm. And from a dollar and 40 cents up to dollar 85 cents. When you reach the age of 70 years old, it cost you $8 a month. What? So I got out of it. So I done made 71 now, so I got out of it, railroad insurance. I stayed in there about 14 years or 15 years. I never seen insurance. The longer you be in there, the the higher it goes up. So I don't belong to the railroad insurance anymore. I worked for the railroad 37 years. All of them were small kids when I first started working for the railroad.
Which railroad is that?
Illinois Central.
What were you doing?
Freightailing.
Did the guys sing when they worked on railroad much?
Not that kind of railroad. Railroad and them fellas shoveling them tires. I didn't do that
in the back. Oh, you didn't do that, man. You didn't hear them.
You used to give me that, that large envelope and that barbacase there. You did? Yeah, looky man. On the top shelf. Is it?
Yeah. So you played with the Eureka, huh?
Yeah, I played Eureka.

I got this here. The Illinois Central Railroad, it says here. February 7, 1956. Dear Sonny, I have a report which informs me that you have retired. Now that your working days are over, I suspect that you will find getting, I suspect this will find you getting a good rest for yourself. You were on the job a long time and worked hard at it. I just wanted you to know of our appreciation for your service with the Illinois Central and to wish you a long and happy retirement. Sincerely yours, W. Johnston. President. Mm-hmm. That's W. A. Johnston. President. That's S-T-O-N.
He's still, he's still President.
That's a nice laugh. You had some time there with him.
Yeah, with all them kids working there. See, when I'd be off playing like over the lake, I'd come back to Boston and have a turn or nothing. It's going back to work. Mm-hmm.
You just take a month off or something if you want?
No, just a few days a week.
Mm-hmm.

Four or five days. You're out and playing, come back, you know, saying that it's going on the way. Plenty of jobs, you couldn't do that here. You don't be there the next day, you ain't got no more jobs. Mm-hmm.
